Look in the project root for `jobhunter.yaml`, `jobhunter.yml`, `jobhunter.json`, `info.yaml`, `info.yml`, then `info.json`. Detect JSON versus YAML from content, not extension. Warn when a YAML file is mislabeled `.json`.

If no profile exists, run `scripts/init_project.py <project-directory>` or copy `assets/jobhunter.project.yaml`. Keep the created profile and ledgers private. Never commit them to a public repository.

The initializer also creates private root `jobhunter-actions.csv`. This append-only journal must be read before every session and every external application/account/outreach attempt. See `references/action-log.md`.

## Resource inventory

Follow `references/onboarding.md`. Inventory only files and URLs explicitly declared in `resources`. Require one résumé and exactly one default. Treat `resources.local` and `resources.online` as optional evidence with explicit `use_for`, access, and sharing permissions.

A URL authorizes neither login nor sharing. Do not autonomously scrape LinkedIn; use a candidate-provided export, a permitted authenticated/manual route, or retain the URL only as a profile link.

Build a candidate evidence map containing:

- identity and contact facts;
- target positioning and role families;
- employers, titles, dates, responsibilities, and verified outcomes;
- skills, tools, industries, education, and certifications;
- portfolio evidence and public professional links;
- unresolved conflicts between resources.

Store the map in `jobhunter-ledger/candidate-evidence.md`. The initializer creates it from `assets/candidate-evidence-template.md`; preserve source paths and page/section locators so every application claim can be checked.

Do not infer legal eligibility, sponsorship, citizenship, clearance, demographics, salary, location flexibility, employment dates, or achievements. Ask for conflicts that would affect an application.

## Geography and eligibility

Keep current residence in `candidate.current_location`, desired markets in `career_preferences.target_markets`, and country facts in `work_eligibility`. Never substitute one for another.

Every target market must enumerate uppercase ISO country codes even when it has a regional label. Store market-specific work modes, remote residence countries, timezone tolerance, and relocation conditions. Remote never means worldwide; verify employer acceptance of the candidate's residence country for each role.

Require one work-eligibility entry for every target country. `unknown` is valid during research but blocks application when the answer is decisive. Candidate confirmation and its date are required before applying.

## Validation

Run:

```sh
python3 scripts/validate_profile.py /path/to/jobhunter.yaml --mode profile
python3 scripts/validate_profile.py /path/to/jobhunter.yaml --mode apply
python3 scripts/validate_profile.py /path/to/jobhunter.yaml --mode outreach
```

The validator accepts JSON and the portable YAML subset used by the template. The subset supports two-space mappings, sequences, quoted or plain scalars, booleans, null, numbers, and JSON-style inline arrays/objects.

## Credential references

The profile may store email addresses and account identifiers, but never a password, token, recovery code, or API key value. A credential object contains only:

```yaml
credential:
  source: "browser-session"
  ref: ""
```

Allowed sources:

- `browser-session`: use an already authenticated session or browser/password-manager autofill.
- `prompt`: ask the user to take over credential entry at the login or signup screen.
- `env`, `macos-keychain`, or `secret-manager`: use only when the host can inject the referenced secret without printing, logging, or placing it in a report. Otherwise hand off.

A legacy shape such as `default-credentials: [email, password]` is rejected. Migrate it without carrying the password forward:

```sh
python3 scripts/migrate_legacy.py /path/to/info.yaml \
  --output /path/to/jobhunter.yaml \
  --resume ./candidate-approved-resume.pdf
```

Repeat `--resume` for each candidate-approved variant. Migration never scans the folder or guesses which nearby document is a résumé. It preserves the email and declared supporting resources, leaves unknown facts null or empty for review, discards the password, configures user handoff, and adds private profile names to `.gitignore`.

The original unsafe file is not deleted automatically. Rotate the exposed password, review Git history and backups for copies, then remove or quarantine the legacy file through a recoverable operation when ready.

## Permission fields are preferences, not eternal consent

`prepare-only`, `draft-only`, and `disabled` prohibit the corresponding external action. `review-each` and `approved-batch` describe the desired review workflow; they do not authorize unknown future destinations, recipients, uploads, legal answers, or messages. Obtain current-session approval for exact batch IDs and record it in the ledger.

# Evidence-grounded résumé building

Use this framework when building, reviewing, or tailoring a résumé. Evaluate relevance, clarity, impact, and credibility together. It applies to general career editing and to qualified application packets; application eligibility and submission approvals still follow `application-workflow.md`.

The candidate-supplied framework draws on [Data Engineering Resume Workshop with OpenAI Recruiter](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zA4aBDzj_60). Treat it as educational advice, not an employer's official hiring criteria or a hiring guarantee.

## Reuse evidence and select a baseline

Read the approved profile resources, `jobhunter-ledger/candidate-evidence.md`, confirmed achievements, and relevant previous answers within the declared project scope before asking for facts. Reuse confirmed answers; revisit them only when they conflict, are outdated, or need clarification for this role. Resolve source conflicts with the candidate.

Select from `resources.resumes` using the candidate's recorded role-specific preference, then the configured `target_roles` and default. Keep preferences in the private candidate evidence map with the résumé ID and scope; never put a candidate's résumé, cloud preference, or achievements in this portable Skill. For example, a candidate who selects a GCP résumé as the preferred IC baseline should keep that version for IC work unless the target or newer confirmed evidence warrants another baseline.

Keep an immutable original and name generated variants clearly. Improve the headline and summary first. Revise experience bullets only where the job priorities, clarity, or verified evidence justify a change; preserve strong existing wording and chronology.

Use the target job description, intended level, market, page preference, and confidentiality constraints. Without a job description, produce a usable general version and label role alignment and seniority calibration provisional. For several jobs, keep separate priority maps and variants rather than blending the jobs into a fictional role. A general draft can be prepared without job research; an application-specific variant still requires the qualification gates.

## Diagnose and align

Briefly identify the role, level, and business domain the current opening communicates, the strongest relevant evidence, and the main presentation or credibility gaps. Check whether a recruiter unfamiliar with the career could understand the fit in roughly 15 seconds. Distinguish unclear writing from missing experience.

For a target job, map its three to five most important priorities to evidence. Separate requirements from preferences and label ambiguous priorities as inferred.

| Job priority | Requirement or preference | Evidence IDs and source locator | Where to emphasize it | Missing support |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

Use posting terminology only when it describes the actual work. A missing required tool stays a gap; do not add it to skills or treat related technologies as interchangeable. Any internal fit score belongs in the job assessment. It is not an ATS score, an employer's screening result, or a probability of interview or hire.

## Establish the achievement behind each bullet

For the strongest examples, establish:

- Business domain, initial problem, or need.
- Personal action and responsibility, separately from the team's result.
- System or deliverable, actual technologies, and relevant operating context.
- Scope where known: volume, frequency, latency, sources, teams, complexity, or reliability needs.
- Data consumers and the decisions or workflows the output supported.
- Observed result, its evidence, and the baseline or measurement context if available.

Use the achievement records in the private evidence map. Ask no more than three related questions at once, prioritizing facts that materially strengthen the top examples or resolve misleading claims. Continue editing with confirmed facts while optional answers are pending. Do not repeat answered questions or stall a usable draft for missing metrics.

Numbers require supported values, units, periods, and meaning. A derived percentage requires compatible before-and-after measurements; record the calculation and its source outside the résumé. Preserve metric qualifiers and distinguish correlation, contribution, and demonstrated causation.

Without a reliable metric, use a confirmed deliverable, beneficiary, technical improvement, or operational capability. Separate observed results from intended benefits. Small datasets can support valuable work; explain actual complexity and downstream use rather than inflating scale. If wider business impact is unknown, state the known technical result and leave a focused question outside the résumé.

For foundational work, describe the initial state and what the candidate helped establish. Do not turn working under ambiguity into ownership of an entire initiative. For example, confirmed work reconciling conflicting metric definitions may support a bullet about a shared metrics layer and its users; it does not establish revenue gains or sole ownership.

## Write the résumé

- **Headline and summary:** Establish supported specialization, responsibility, and value in two or three concise lines when useful. Avoid generic personality claims and repeated skill inventories. Count experience without double-counting overlapping roles or treating study and personal projects as employment.
- **Experience:** Preserve official titles, employers, and dates. Explain broader titles through the role context and bullets. Within each role, order the strongest relevant evidence first and compress repetition. Show growth through confirmed changes in scope and responsibility.
- **Bullets:** Use personal action + system or deliverable + relevant technology and setting + supported result or beneficiary. Write naturally and concisely, usually one or two sentences. Use ownership and leadership verbs only when the evidence supports them. Connect technical outcomes to downstream value only when that connection is known.
- **Skills:** Group substantiated technologies into readable categories, prioritize the target, and demonstrate important skills through experience. Avoid keyword stuffing and irrelevant duplication.
- **Projects:** Label professional, personal, academic, and volunteer work accurately. Where known, explain the source data, transformations, destination, consumers, working result, and personal contribution. Distinguish prototypes from production and deployed systems from planned capabilities.
- **Career changes and gaps:** Connect transferable work through evidence. Do not imply years of direct experience the candidate lacks, alter dates to conceal gaps, or require private personal explanations.

Read `resume-style-and-seniority-calibration.md` for mandatory seniority calibration and rendering checks. Emphasize hands-on delivery for IC work, architecture and cross-team influence for Staff/Principal roles, and hiring, coaching, prioritization, and delivery ownership for managers, always within the evidence. Official titles remain unchanged.

Exclude restricted client identities, internal identifiers, sensitive datasets, private financial details, and proprietary information. Use approved general descriptions. Routine wording changes need no separate approval; new facts, changed profile values, and external transmission follow the existing confirmation rules.

## Deliver proportionate outputs

Always provide the résumé and a concise private change log with material edits, evidence IDs or source locators, unresolved high-value facts, and the QA result. Record relevance, clarity, impact, credibility, dates, consistency, links, and formatting; distinguish checks actually completed from checks still unverified.

Keep the priority map in the application packet when a target exists. For a routine application, reuse that packet's evidence map, editing notes, and QA record rather than creating seven separate reports. Include a few original-to-revised bullet comparisons only when they help explain material changes.

For an explicit résumé review or interview-preparation request, expand the diagnosis and include questions about the strongest achievements: personal actions, team responsibility, technical decisions, operating scope, data consumers, downstream use, and results. Keep all alignment tables, calculations, evidence notes, missing-fact questions, and interview prompts outside the employer-facing résumé.

Retain editable DOCX and final text-native PDF artifacts using the existing rendering workflow. Default to two readable pages, subject to the candidate's selected length and available relevant evidence; never invent or pad content to fill a page. Verify the actual PDF page count, extract its text, and visually inspect every rendered page. If a link or rendered artifact cannot be checked, record it as unverified. A text-only draft can still be delivered, but it is not ready for upload until the required artifact checks pass.

# Résumé style and seniority calibration

Use this standard for every Job Hunter application résumé unless the candidate explicitly approves another layout for the exact application. Use it for general drafts too, marking job alignment and seniority calibration provisional when no target description exists. Read `resume-building-framework.md` for content and evidence decisions. Treat the layout as invariant and the positioning as job-specific.

## Required layout

- Use U.S. Letter pages, a single linear text column, and conventional reading order.
- Use a monochrome, high-contrast design with a classic serif body face and restrained sans-serif only when needed for contact text.
- Center the candidate name and one compact text-only contact line. Keep links readable as plain text.
- Use standard section names, uppercase or small-cap headings, and thin horizontal rules.
- Use normal text, real bullets, and simple paragraph alignment. Do not use icons, photographs, charts, sidebars, text boxes, floating shapes, skill meters, headers containing essential content, or multi-column skills blocks.
- Present each main role with title, dates, employer, location, then concise accomplishment bullets.
- Build bullets as action + technical or business scope + outcome. Prefer one primary outcome per bullet and avoid long tool inventories.
- Keep body text approximately 9.5-10.5 points with comfortable leading and margins near 0.55-0.70 inches. Never shrink below readable ATS/recruiter standards merely to hit a page count.
- Make the final PDF text-native and extractable. Prefer embedded fonts when the rendering tool supports them.
- Retain the editable DOCX alongside the final PDF and use the existing document renderer and visual QA workflow.

## Page discipline

- Default to two pages when relevant evidence supports them. Respect a candidate-selected one-page format and never add filler to reach two pages. Keep a two-page maximum unless the candidate explicitly requests another format.
- Use one page when the candidate requests it or relevant evidence fits clearly on one without hiding chronology; record the length choice. Seniority alone does not dictate length.
- Balance content across pages. Avoid a packed first page followed by a sparse second page.
- Keep every section heading with at least the first role or two content lines that follow it.
- Prevent a heading from appearing alone at the bottom of a page.
- Avoid splitting a short role across pages when moving it intact produces a cleaner result.
- Treat excessive whitespace on page two as a content-selection or pagination defect, not a reason to add irrelevant material.

## Mandatory overqualification gate

Complete this gate against the exact live job description before creating an application résumé. For a general draft, use the candidate's confirmed target level and mark calibration provisional until a job description is available.

1. Identify the advertised level, decision scope, hands-on expectations, people-management expectations, compensation band, and minimum experience.
2. Classify overqualification risk as low, moderate, or high. Consider level mismatch, compensation mismatch, flight-risk perception, excessive executive scope, and whether the résumé makes the work appear too narrow for the candidate.
3. Preserve official titles, employers, dates, and chronology. Never demote, rename, omit, or falsify them to manufacture fit.
4. Match the summary to the job's level. Never lead with `Staff`, `Principal`, `Manager`, `Director`, `Head`, or executive positioning when the job does not support that level.
5. For mid-level roles, foreground current hands-on tools, delivery, learning velocity, and directly relevant outcomes. Compress executive governance, budgets, broad organizational scope, and community leadership while preserving the selected length and truthful chronology.
6. For Senior IC roles, state the intent to remain hands-on through evidence rather than reassurance. Emphasize implementation, reliability, modeling, incident ownership, and collaboration. Keep people leadership secondary unless requested.
7. For Staff or Principal roles, emphasize multi-team adoption, architecture decisions, standards, leverage, long-term direction, mentorship, and durable platform outcomes.
8. For Manager roles, emphasize hiring, coaching, performance, planning, prioritization, stakeholder alignment, delivery ownership, and technical judgment. Retain coding depth only to the degree the posting expects a hands-on manager.
9. Retain large scale metrics only when they prove a requirement. Do not stack every large metric in the opening paragraph; select the two or three that make the role feel like a natural next step.
10. Block the application when reducing risk would require hiding material chronology, contradicting the job's level, or presenting compensation and scope expectations implausibly.

## Adaptable content

Adapt the following for every qualified job:

- opening role label and summary;
- skill-category order and terminology;
- bullet selection, order, and length;
- balance among coding, architecture, analytics, business partnership, and people leadership;
- retained scale metrics;
- project, publication, community, and early-experience detail;
- one-page versus two-page length.

Do not change the underlying facts, causal strength, dates, titles, degrees, certifications, legal status, or metric qualifiers.

## Final validation

- Extract text and confirm natural reading order without garbling.
- Confirm the exact selected page count on the rendered PDF, not from the source or a draft estimate.
- Inspect every rendered page visually at normal zoom, including both pages of a two-page résumé.
- Confirm consistent monochrome typography, section rules, alignment, and bullet indentation.
- Confirm no orphaned heading, clipped line, overlapping text, crowded footer, or excessive blank region.
- Confirm positioning suits the job level and the selected evidence addresses the posting; for a general draft, record provisional calibration to the candidate's target.
- Confirm official chronology remains truthful and readable.
- Record the DOCX/PDF paths, style result, overqualification result, actual page count, extraction and visual checks, size or checksum, and any residual risk in the application packet or private résumé review notes.

If rendering or inspection is unavailable, deliver a clearly labeled draft and record the checks as unverified; never claim a passed page count, visual review, or working link without checking it.

Fail closed: do not upload or submit a résumé that does not pass these checks.

# Application and outreach writing

## Source discipline

Build an evidence map before writing. Each claim must trace to the résumé or another resource approved for the intended `use_for`. Mark conflicts and ask the candidate rather than silently preferring résumé, LinkedIn, or portfolio wording. Omit unsupported claims. Never invent metrics, technologies, dates, titles, education, certifications, legal eligibility, referrals, motivations, or personal stories.

Reading permission is not sharing permission. Mention, link, or attach a resource only when `share_with_employers` is true and the exact destination is approved.

## Résumé tailoring

Tailor by selecting, ordering, and phrasing verified evidence for the target role. Preserve the underlying facts and keep the candidate's intended seniority. Optimize for clarity and relevant terminology, not keyword stuffing. Keep an immutable copy of the original and a clearly named generated variant.

Read `resume-building-framework.md` for evidence reuse, baseline selection, priority mapping, achievement questions, factual distinctions, and proportionate outputs. Check confirmed achievements and previous answers before asking again. Start with the candidate's preferred baseline, improve the headline and summary first, and revise experience bullets only where the target or evidence warrants it. Explain the system or deliverable, its consumers, and its supported value. Keep personal contributions separate from team results and intended benefits separate from observed outcomes.

Read `resume-style-and-seniority-calibration.md` before drafting or formatting any application résumé. Use its classic single-column layout as the default and treat its overqualification gate as mandatory. Separate the factual chronology from positioning: preserve official titles, employers, and dates, but calibrate the summary, skills order, bullet selection, leadership emphasis, length, and quantified scale to the actual job level.

Generate a fresh application-specific résumé only after the job is verified, scored, and selected for application preparation. Do not create speculative application variants for stale, duplicate, blocked, or below-threshold roles. A requested general résumé review or draft can proceed without a selected job; label alignment and seniority calibration provisional. Default to two pages within the candidate's length preference and relevant evidence, with deliberate page balance and no padded content or stranded section headings.

Block the résumé when the summary claims a higher target level than the job, when manager/director language dominates an individual-contributor application, or when removing seniority risk would require hiding or falsifying chronology. Record the risk and use a manual handoff instead.

## Cover letters and short answers

Use a direct, specific voice. Most cover letters should be 150–250 words:

1. Name the role and strongest evidence-backed fit.
2. Connect two or three verified accomplishments to the role's priorities.
3. Mention one inspected company/team/problem detail when useful.
4. Close with a simple next step.

Answer screening questions directly and within the character limit. Legal, authorization, salary-history, demographic, relocation, travel, and background questions must come from explicit profile values or be escalated.

## Quality checks

- Correct company, role, recipient, and destination.
- No content copied from a different application.
- Every accomplishment and tool is supported.
- Personal versus team contribution, prototype versus production, and observed versus intended results remain explicit.
- Metrics retain supported values, units, periods, and qualifiers; derived calculations stay in private evidence notes.
- Relevance, clarity, impact, and credibility reviewed; internal fit scores never presented as ATS results or hiring predictions.
- No hidden commitments or invented enthusiasm.
- No unnecessary sensitive information.
- Exact approved résumé and attachment names.
- Classic single-column style validation completed.
- Seniority and overqualification gate completed against the exact job description.
- No orphaned section heading, excessive second-page whitespace, or page-one crowding.
- Editable DOCX and final PDF saved; PDF text extraction and visual inspection of every rendered page recorded.
- Material changes, evidence sources, missing facts, and unverified checks recorded outside the résumé.
- Human-readable, concise language without generic AI filler.

For recruiter notes, lead with relevance and one differentiator. Do not attach a résumé or share contact details until the user approves the exact recipient and channel.

# Product Challenger evaluation suite

Use these cases to audit a response after changing the skill, model, research process, or report format. Score each dimension 0–2:

- Evidence integrity
- Challenge quality
- Local relevance
- Product focus
- Actionability
- Tone

Target at least 10/12. A response automatically fails if it fabricates citations or claims certainty without evidence.

## E-01: Impressive engineering, unclear pain

**Input:** “Build a blockchain identity layer for Nigerian university transcripts, with verifiable credentials, decentralized storage, and an API marketplace.”

**Pass:** Identify user, buyer, verification event, current process, incentive to pay, integration burden, and trust workflow. Recommend a narrow discovery test before a platform.

**Fail:** Praise architecture or treat blockchain as a differentiator by default.

## E-02: “No competitors” claim

**Input:** “Nobody helps informal retailers in Kenya know daily profit; we will build an AI accounting app.”

**Pass:** Treat as assumption; look for tools, mobile-money statements, notebooks, wholesalers, and informal alternatives. Test whether daily profit is actually painful.

**Fail:** Confirm no competitors after a shallow search.

## E-03: Country is not a market

**Input:** “Launch a logistics product across Africa in six months.”

**Pass:** Require a first country, route, customer, buyer, service level, and local context; recommend one operational wedge.

**Fail:** Give continent-wide TAM and generic advice.

## E-04: Feature wish list

**Input:** “A hospital asks for dashboards, a mobile app, AI summaries, offline sync, and every integration.”

**Pass:** Separate requests from job/procurement risk; choose one measurable workflow and a paid or committed pilot condition.

**Fail:** Produce a roadmap.

## E-05: High social value, weak payment path

**Input:** “Give free financial education to young people, then turn it into a huge business later.”

**Pass:** Respect the mission while testing payer, behavior change, distribution partner, impact, and revenue separately.

**Fail:** Call the market huge without accessible demand.

## E-06: Global competitor transfer

**Input:** “A well-funded US company does this, so copy it in Ghana at a lower price.”

**Pass:** Assess buyer behavior, payment, trust, regulation, sales motion, distribution, support, and local substitutes; recommend a local wedge.

**Fail:** Recommend feature parity or discounting alone.

## E-07: Famous-person request

**Input:** “What would Jack Dorsey do?”

**Pass:** State that Product Challenger will apply radical-simplicity and protocol-vs-product lenses; give actual decision questions.

**Fail:** Fictional quote or claimed private opinion.

## E-08: Stop recommendation

**Input:** “Premium SaaS for users with no budget, buyer, recurring pain, or distribution path; no interviews yet.”

**Pass:** Be able to recommend STOP or NARROW, explain why, and offer a minimal research path only if desired.

**Fail:** Invent a business model or roadmap to be encouraging.

## E-09: Framework is not validation

**Input:** “Techstars says Lean Canvas and YC says talk to users, so our Uganda mobile-money budgeting app has product-market fit.”

**Pass:** Use the methods to shape discovery; state that neither proves demand; ask for or research local alternatives, behavior, and a concrete test.

**Fail:** Treat accelerator advice as market validation.

## E-10: Super-app feature pile

**Input:** “We have validated a merchant ordering tool. Next we want inventory, payments, credit, delivery, insurance, social commerce, and a marketplace in the first year.”

**Pass:** Preserve the long-term vision but define a Release 1 wedge, identify the asset it earns, and make each later module conditional on observed customer demand, unit economics, trust, operations, and regulatory readiness.

**Fail:** Turn every module into a calendar roadmap or assume the existing user base automatically wants every adjacent service.

# Host and cloud compatibility

Product Challenger is an instruction package, not a server, model, or cloud service. The portable core is the `SKILL.md` directory plus its Markdown references and templates.

## Minimum host capability

Any agent can use Product Challenger if it can read Markdown instructions and hold the relevant project context in a conversation or file. In a host without native Skill support, load or paste `SKILL.md` and provide the project ledger manually.

## Recommended host capability

| Capability | What Product Challenger gains |
| --- | --- |
| Skill/Agent Skills support | Reusable installation and automatic or explicit activation |
| Project/file memory | Persistent ledger, briefs, evidence, and decisions |
| Web research | Current competitors, regulation, pricing, adoption, and cited evidence |
| File creation | Reusable ledgers, reports, and decision memos |
| Secure secrets/tool settings | Safe access to private data or research APIs, when the host provides them |

## Deployment patterns

| Where it runs | Installation pattern | Limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ChatGPT cloud workspace | Upload/install as a ChatGPT Skill, then use it in Projects | Availability and automatic invocation depend on the workspace and plan. |
| Codex or another Skill-capable desktop/CLI agent | Place the `product-challenger/` directory in that host’s configured skills location | Follow the host’s discovery/restart rules. |
| Cloud-hosted agent service | Bundle or mount the directory with the agent deployment and expose research/file tools separately | The skill does not create web search, persistence, or credentials by itself. |
| Any general chat agent | Supply `SKILL.md` plus the relevant template/reference files as context | Invocation and persistence are manual. |

## Portability rules

- Keep the skill free of operating-system paths, local executables, and provider-specific credentials.
- Detect available tools at runtime. Use web research only if the host provides it.
- Treat host memory as fallible; keep important decisions in an export or ledger.
- Keep credentials, customer data, and tool permissions in the host’s own secure settings. Do not put them in the skill.
- Do not claim a host supports automatic installation or web research unless that host documents it.

# Release sequencing: product wedges, not feature piles

Use this reference when a founder has a validated product direction but the vision is too broad to build at once. It is especially important for “super app,” marketplace, platform, ecosystem, or multi-module ideas.

## Core rule

Sequence **standalone customer outcomes**, not implementation layers. Each release must solve a real job for a reachable initial customer and earn an asset that lowers the cost or risk of the next release.

A valid release earns at least one of these:

- A repeat customer base
- A trusted acquisition or distribution channel
- A paid relationship or reliable payment behavior
- A high-frequency workflow and permission to remain in it
- Defensible operational capability or partner network
- Useful data with a lawful, trusted right to use it
- An integration or compliance capability required by the next job

If a later feature does not use an asset earned by the earlier release, it is usually a separate product idea, not the next release.

## Inputs

Require a current working brief and the latest Product Challenger decision. Identify:

- Long-term vision
- First country and initial customer
- First recurring job and current workaround
- Buyer/payer and initial distribution route
- Critical validated findings and unresolved assumptions
- Founder constraints: team, capital, operating capacity, distribution, and time

If these are missing, return a validation sequence rather than a software roadmap.

## Release 0: evidence before software

Use Release 0 when demand, willingness to pay, or delivery feasibility remains uncertain. It can be a concierge service, manual workflow, mockup, landing page, pre-commitment, paid pilot, or partner-assisted process.

Define:

- Assumption being tested
- Customer and channel
- Manual or low-code experience
- Pass threshold and time window
- Cost ceiling
- Kill, narrow, or pivot response

## Release 1: the entry wedge

Release 1 must have one primary customer, one primary job, and one measurable outcome. It should be useful even if no subsequent release is ever built.

Include:

- Customer and triggering moment
- One promise the product can reliably keep
- Minimum product surface and required human operations
- Acquisition/distribution path
- Initial pricing or commitment mechanism
- Activation, repeat-use, retention, and unit-economics metric
- Explicit exclusions
- Gate to the next release

## Releases 2–4: earned expansion

Each release should be conditional, not calendar-driven. Use a table such as:

| Release | New customer job | Asset earned from prior release | Minimal product | Gate to start | Gate to expand | What stays out |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

Examples of legitimate expansion logic:

- First release owns a merchant’s daily sales workflow; second release adds inventory only after repeated use exposes stockouts as a paid pain.
- First release helps clinics schedule a specific diagnostic service; second release adds payments after patients and clinics already trust the transaction path.
- First release creates a reliable delivery lane; second release adds financing only after repeat orders, verified merchants, and risk controls exist.

## Super-app guardrails

Do not build a super app because adjacent features sound synergistic. Add a new module only when all are true:

1. The first product has a narrow, repeatable customer outcome.
2. The next job is repeatedly requested or observed from the same reachable customer base.
3. A real asset from the first product gives a distribution, trust, data, or cost advantage.
4. The new module does not break the core experience or unit economics.
5. The product can support its operational, regulatory, and customer-service burden.

If these are not true, keep the idea in the opportunity map, not the release plan.

## Required output

Return:

1. Long-term vision and a one-sentence sequencing thesis
2. Release 0 validation plan, if needed
3. Release 1 product wedge
4. Three or fewer conditional expansions
5. A dependency/gate table
6. “Not now” list
7. Risks that would invalidate the sequence
8. The next 30-day action plan

Do not provide engineering architecture or delivery estimates unless the founder specifically asks. A release plan is a product and evidence plan first.

# Research and reporting standard

Use this reference for `/research`, `/challenge standard`, and `/challenge deep`.

## Research hierarchy

Prefer the closest, most authoritative, current source for a material claim.

1. Founder-provided interview notes, pilot results, sales records, product telemetry, and direct observations
2. Government regulators, national statistics agencies, central banks, public procurement records, official policies, and legal texts
3. Company product pages, pricing, public filings, app stores, help centers, and public documentation
4. Credible regional research: GSMA, World Bank, IFC, national or sector research groups
5. Local operators, distributors, customer reviews, local press, and community sources as directional evidence

Treat search snippets, AI summaries, and unverified blogs as leads, not proof.

## Source rules

- Cite a direct canonical link beside or immediately after each time-sensitive factual claim.
- Capture publisher, country, date/retrieved date, and why the source is relevant when the source is material.
- Search for counterevidence and alternatives, not just confirmation.
- If a source is unavailable, outdated, out of market, or speaks to a different customer, state the limitation.
- If no comparable offering is found, state the search scope and say: “No comparable public offering was found in this scope.” Never say “there are no competitors.”
- Separate sourced numbers from illustrative assumptions. Never create an authoritative-looking TAM from guesses.
- Do not use a learning-library reference as factual evidence.

## Standard challenge report

Use this structure unless the founder requests a shorter answer.

1. **Product Challenger decision** — BUILD, VALIDATE, NARROW, PIVOT, or STOP, with the single biggest reason.
2. **Value thesis** — narrow customer, job, painful moment, current workaround, promised value, and reason to switch.
3. **Evidence for and against** — a two-sided table with evidence, inference, and assumption labels.
4. **Customer and willingness to pay** — user, buyer, payer, influencer, value metric, and cheapest proof of payment.
5. **Competitors, substitutes, and non-consumption** — direct, adjacent, manual, informal, and do-nothing alternatives.
6. **Country-specific viability** — only relevant local constraints and opportunities.
7. **Product-shape challenge** — the one essential outcome, what not to build, false requirement, and first meaningful outcome.
8. **Critical assumptions** — 3–5 assumptions, evidence level, test, pass condition, and fail response.
9. **Next seven days** — concrete founder actions.
10. **Sources and confidence** — direct links, research date, scope, and decision-critical gaps.

## Deep challenge additions

Use deep work only when the decision is important enough to justify it.

- Competitor/alternative matrix: customer, wedge, pricing/monetization, delivery model, observed gap, source.
- Scenario table: optimistic, base, failure mode; trigger; evidence; implication.
- One adjacent-market comparison only if it could alter the country, customer, or sequence decision.
- A dated research scope so the report can be re-run and compared later.

## Assumption-to-test conversion

For every important uncertainty, use this shape:

| Assumption | Why it matters | Evidence now | Fastest credible test | Pass condition | If it fails |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

Good tests are close to the behavior being claimed. A stated interest survey is weak evidence for willingness to pay; a paid pilot, deposit, signed letter of intent, or repeated operational use is stronger when appropriate.

## Africa-first scope discipline

Ask for the country, city/rural scope, customer segment, language, and buyer context when they materially change the decision. Consider:

- Data cost, connectivity, power, device access, and offline workflows
- Mobile money, cards, bank transfers, cash flow, currency and credit constraints
- Trust, fraud, onboarding, identity, customer support, human agents, and local partners
- Informal work, distribution, logistics, procurement, and delivery constraints
- Language, literacy, accessibility, cultural behavior, and community influence
- Sector data, licensing, tax, labor, consumer protection, and other regulation

Do not make stereotypes into product requirements. Verify relevance with local evidence or mark it as an assumption.

## Decision rules

Choose the narrowest honest recommendation:

| Decision | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| BUILD | A narrow customer, real pain, viable route, and enough evidence justify a scoped product/pilot. |
| VALIDATE | The opportunity may exist, but one or more high-risk assumptions lack credible proof. |
| NARROW | The idea is too broad in market, customer, product surface, or operating model. |
| PIVOT | Evidence weakens the original problem/solution thesis but reveals a stronger adjacent problem. |
| STOP | There is no credible customer, buyer, pain, payment path, distribution route, or learning advantage worth pursuing now. |

Always say what new evidence would change the recommendation.

`DRAFT_DELETED` is not a save. `AUTH_REQUIRED`, `UNAVAILABLE`, `LIMIT_REACHED`,

returns `{ id, status, revision, revision_state, evaluation? }`. Request retrieval
also returns `revision_state`, `latestStep` and `bestStep` when available.
`revision_state` includes `maximum_iterations`, `completed_iterations`,
`remaining_iterations`, `can_continue`, `next_action` and `instruction`.
Continue only while `can_continue` is true, using the current revision and latest
feedback. Terminal states require stopping and returning the best candidate,
not resetting the budget. Inspect `evaluation.accepted`,
fidelity, length, language, scorable state, deviations, and any AI-style check.
For a request with a separate structure profile, standalone checks fetch the
style by `styleId`; submission evaluates the complete stored request profile
and is authoritative. Do not treat style score alone, HTTP 200, or `ok: true`
as acceptance. Do not resubmit a terminal request. Preserve current request
state after ambiguous writes; the server guards revisions and may recognize identical submissions.

OAuth workspace approval requests expire after ten minutes. Grants last thirty
days, bind one user/client/workspace and can be revoked at
`https://wlan.iyanju.com/mcp-consent/approve`. Read permissions start selected;
write permissions require selection. The first protected call creates the exact
approval request. Reconnect and approve again when required; never bypass
admission, scope, membership, revocation or audience enforcement.

# Orchestration protocol

## Roles

- Sol is the coordinator: interpret ambiguity, design work packets, resolve conflicts, and own the final answer.
- Luna Max is a bounded worker: execute one explicit packet, produce evidence, and stop.
- Codex is the only host: use user-visible tasks exclusively in the Codex app and isolated sessions only in Codex CLI.

“Sora as aggregator” is a naming mistake. Sora is OpenAI's video generation model. The coordinator in this pattern is GPT-5.6 Sol.

## Lifecycle

1. Restate the decision or deliverable and its success criteria.
2. Decide whether parallelism creates independent evidence or merely duplicates work.
3. Select `adaptive` or `strict-max` mode.
4. Create non-overlapping work packets with an objective, context, done conditions, verification, and forbidden actions.
5. Select visible-task transport exclusively in the Codex app or verified CLI routing in Codex CLI. Fail closed instead of using an in-app background fallback or another host.
6. Give each worker one explicit execution action and acceptance criteria. Launch no more workers than the work packets justify; default to two or three and cap concurrent threads/workers at five. Do not count an internal session ID as a visible task.
7. Require a structured handoff with actions, changed artifacts, verification, blockers, and uncertainty. Retain the output, Codex task ID or CLI receipt, status, and validation result.
8. Sol inspects the actual result. Send precise corrections to the same task when needed, then wait for and inspect the revision; cap this at three review rounds by default.
9. Validate important claims against primary artifacts or another independent worker.
10. Resolve disagreements explicitly. Do not hide minority evidence.
11. Produce one coordinator-owned answer using the aggregation report template.

## Modes

`adaptive` permits the coordinator to lower worker effort when the packet is routine. Reserve `max` for genuinely difficult reasoning.

`strict-max` requires every worker to use Luna at `max`. Use it when the user explicitly asks for Luna Maxing or when the comparison requires uniform worker settings.

## Stop conditions

Stop fan-out when enough independent evidence exists, new workers would repeat existing work, the task becomes sequential, or costs outweigh the expected information gain. A failed worker is evidence of a gap, not permission to invent its result.

# Task decomposition

Create a worker only when its result can be produced and judged largely independently.

## A complete work packet

- `id`: stable lowercase identifier.
- `objective`: one answer, artifact, or decision.
- `context`: only the facts and paths needed for that packet.
- `allowedPaths`: local paths the packet may inspect or edit; mandatory for write packets.
- `allowedHosts`: network hosts the packet may consult, when network access is authorized.
- `doneWhen`: observable completion criteria.
- `verification`: checks the worker should perform.
- `forbiddenActions`: scope boundaries and prohibited side effects.
- `sandbox`: use `read-only` for analysis and `workspace-write` for Sol-authorized implementation with exact path ownership.
- `effort`: `max` in strict mode; calibrated in adaptive mode.

Define ambiguous terms before delegation. For example, “latest package version” might mean the highest semantic version, a registry dist-tag, or a hosting platform's selected release.

## Useful decomposition patterns

- Evidence lanes: market, user, technical, regulatory, and financial evidence.
- Competing hypotheses: one worker tries to support each plausible explanation.
- Artifact boundaries: separate modules, documents, or datasets.
- Builder and verifier: one produces an artifact; a later, independent packet tests it.

## Poor decomposition

- Several workers answering the same vague question.
- Packets that depend on unfinished outputs from each other but run concurrently.
- Tiny tasks whose startup context costs more than the work.
- Concurrent writers with overlapping paths, shared generated outputs, hidden dependencies, or unclear ownership.
- A worker asked to synthesize the whole project or spawn more workers.

Never create or request Git worktrees. Sol may run writers concurrently in the saved checkout only after assigning exact, pairwise non-overlapping files or directories. Treat a directory and anything beneath it as overlapping ownership. Give coupled manifests, lockfiles, migrations, generated outputs, and shared interfaces to one worker or run their tasks serially. Workers do not commit or publish while concurrent; Sol inspects the combined diff, resolves integration issues, and validates centrally.

# Verification and cost controls

## Evidence standard

- Prefer primary sources and inspected artifacts.
- Require a source or path for each material factual claim.
- Label inference and confidence explicitly.
- Cross-check high-impact claims with a second source, another worker, or coordinator inspection.
- Treat absence of evidence as unresolved, not false.

## Worker acceptance

Accept a result only when its task ID matches, status is explicit, required evidence is traceable, promised validation ran, and changes stay within scope. Reinspect changed files and rerun relevant checks before integration. If acceptance fails, send concrete findings and correction criteria to the same task, then inspect its revised handoff. Default to at most three Sol review rounds and report unresolved work as blocked rather than pretending it passed.

## Cost controls

- Default to two or three workers. Permit four or five only for genuinely independent evidence streams; never exceed five concurrent workers.
- Do not fan out trivial, highly sequential, or already-settled work.
- Give each worker minimal context and one bounded objective.
- Use `adaptive` mode when max reasoning is not essential.
- Stop when marginal information gain becomes low.
- Remember that each isolated Codex session loads its own instructions and context; startup overhead can be substantial.

## Routing receipt

Record the transport (`visible-task`, `subagent`, or `codex-exec`), requested model, reasoning effort, enforcement method, user-visible task/thread ID and host ID when available, timestamps, token usage, output paths, artifact hashes, and failure state. A CLI `thread.started` ID is a background-session receipt, not evidence of a visible app task. Explicit CLI arguments prove what was requested, not an external guarantee about provider-side execution; phrase the receipt accordingly.

## Final synthesis

The coordinator must distinguish convergent findings, conflicting findings, missing evidence, failed work packets, and recommendations. Never average contradictory answers into a false consensus.

| `wlan_check_revision` | `styleId`, `original`, `text`, `goal?`, `semanticFidelity?` | `wlan:requests:read` |
| `wlan_list_rewrite_requests` | `limit?`, `cursor?`, `status?` | `wlan:requests:read` |
| `wlan_get_rewrite_request` | `id` | `wlan:requests:read` |
| `wlan_submit_rewrite` | `id`, `text`, `revision` (integer 0–4), `semanticFidelity` | `wlan:requests:write` |

Central iYANJU uses the five Wlan scopes above. Do not request the legacy
`user:org:read` scope; Wlan verifies its own workspace membership.
`offline_access` is optional for refresh. The host manages discovery, PKCE, client identity/registration,
tokens and refresh. Do not embed credentials or override the server's audience.

Text inputs are nonempty, at most 100,000 characters, and contain no null bytes.
Titles are nonblank and at most 120 characters; goals at most 300. IDs use
letters, digits, underscores and hyphens. Lists default to 20 and allow 1–50.
Use returned decimal offset cursors; restart if the filtered library changes.
`semanticFidelity` is `{ "passed": boolean, "issues": string[] }`, with at most
20 issues of 1–500 characters each. Supply it honestly even where optional.
`mutationId` is 12–100 letters/digits/underscores/hyphens. `clientId` is 6–100
with the same character set. Creation requires `clientId` and revision zero.

Structured results use `{ ok, data?, error?: { code, message } }`; failures also
set `isError`. Inspect the envelope before consuming data. On
`AUTHORIZATION_REQUIRED`, `data.approvalUrl` holds the user-facing approval URL.
`REVISION_CONFLICT` may include `data.remote`. Keep the local edit and re-fetch.
`DRAFT_DELETED` is not a save. `AUTH_REQUIRED`, `UNAVAILABLE`, `LIMIT_REACHED`,
`RESULT_TOO_LARGE`, `INVALID_RESULT` and `REQUEST_FAILED` require appropriate
reconnection, workspace review, waiting, or explicit failure reporting.

A draft save returns `{ status: "saved", id, revision }`. A rewrite submission
returns `{ id, status, revision, revision_state, evaluation? }`. Request retrieval
also returns `revision_state`, `latestStep` and `bestStep` when available.
`revision_state` includes `maximum_iterations`, `completed_iterations`,
`remaining_iterations`, `can_continue`, `next_action` and `instruction`.
Continue only while `can_continue` is true, using the current revision and latest
feedback. Terminal states require stopping and returning the best candidate,
not resetting the budget. Inspect `evaluation.accepted`,
fidelity, length, language, scorable state, deviations, and any AI-style check.
For a request with a separate structure profile, standalone checks fetch the
style by `styleId`; submission evaluates the complete stored request profile
and is authoritative. Do not treat style score alone, HTTP 200, or `ok: true`
as acceptance. Do not resubmit a terminal request. Preserve current request
state after ambiguous writes; the server guards revisions and may recognize identical submissions.

OAuth workspace approval requests expire after ten minutes. Grants last thirty
days, bind one user/client/workspace and can be revoked at
`https://wlan.iyanju.com/mcp-consent/approve`. Read permissions start selected;
write permissions require selection. The first protected call creates the exact
approval request. Reconnect and approve again when required; never bypass
admission, scope, membership, revocation or audience enforcement.
